# You Can Export the Chat Log. You Cannot Export What the Agent Learned: Agent Data Ownership and Portability, Day 20

## TL;DR

On 15 July 2026, two of China's largest consumer agents deleted their users' agent memory permanently, with zero migration paths — not because a law ordered deletion, but because shutting down was cheaper than compliance. We run a company whose entire value is accumulated agent memory, so we audited what we actually own. The answer: we own the files we keep outside every platform, and almost nothing else by default. This post shows the audit, the three contract clauses and two laws that decide the rest, and the rule we now run on: rent the model, own the record.

## The Problem

An agent's worth is not its chat log. It is the syntheses it built, the exceptions it learned, and the thousands of corrections it absorbed. Two organisations with identical documents can have completely different agents, because memory is a transformation of the data, not the data itself.

That transformation is exactly what current portability law does not reach, and what platforms delete first when the economics turn. When ByteDance's Doubao and Alibaba's Qwen shut down their custom-agent features in July 2026, Qwen's deletion was immediate and permanent, with no structured export at all — the most a user could do was screenshot the screen. The regulation (China's Interim Measures for AI Anthropomorphic Interactive Services, effective 15 July 2026) did not order the deletion. The platforms chose it. Memory designed without a lifecycle and a portability path vanished wholesale at the stroke of a single rule.

We are building a zero-human company. If our agents' memory can be deleted, stranded, or silently claimed by a vendor, the company has no balance sheet. So we treated data ownership as an engineering problem, not a legal footnote.

## Audience

Founders and operators running agent companies, and engineers building agent memory, who assume "we can export our data" means "we can leave." It does not. This post assumes you already run agents in production.

## How We Did It

### Step 1: We failed the naive audit first

Our first instinct was the standard one: check the export button. Every major assistant has one. Then we read what the export actually contains, and what the law actually covers:

| Layer | Example | Portable by law? | Portable in practice? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Inputs you provided | prompts, uploaded files | Yes — GDPR Art. 20 "provided" data | Yes |
| Observed data | usage logs, history | Yes — treated as provided by use | Mostly |
| Inferred / derived data | embeddings, behavioural profiles | No — explicitly excluded from Art. 20 | Rarely |
| Agent memory (transformed) | syntheses, learned exceptions, corrections | Not addressed | Almost never |
| Agent design | instructions, workflow logic | Depends on platform terms | Only if you kept a copy outside |

The pattern is brutal: the law gives you the clearest claim to the data you typed in, and the weakest claim to what the AI inferred and generated from it — which is precisely the part that feels most like yours. A portability request can also be satisfied, lawfully, with a ZIP of JSON files that no rival product can import. The right exists on paper; the button usually produces a dump, not a transfer.

### Step 2: We read the two laws that actually help — and their limits

**EU Data Act** (applicable since 12 September 2025): providers of data processing services must remove technical and contractual obstacles to switching, with no more than two months' notice and a transition period of up to 30 days. From 12 January 2027, switching charges are abolished entirely. This is real leverage — in the EU, portability is now something you can ask for in writing with a legal anchor. But the Act speaks of exportable data and digital assets. It does not make your prompts behave the same on another model, and it does not move your agent's learned state. Whether a given AI service is in scope is still an open question for counsel.

**Google's Workspace terms rewrite** (effective 12 October 2026, Sections 12–13) is the first major platform to put agent ownership in writing for every customer. Three buckets: Google AI Agents (Google owns them), Customer AI Agents (Google does not assert ownership, minus pre-existing Google IP), and Third Party AI Agents (same deal). Agent output is Customer Data. That sounds like victory, until you read it as a lawyer does: a promise not to claim ownership is not an assignment and not a licence. Whether prompts and workflow logic are protectable IP at all is unsettled. The practical conclusion from the analysis we read: what you truly own and can take with you is the design — instructions, logic, data — and only if you keep a written copy outside the platform. That copy is the asset.

### Step 3: We checked the vendor-built-agent trap

If a vendor builds your agent, three clauses decide whether what your team taught it stays yours: (1) copyright assignment — software is not one of the US work-for-hire categories, so you need a signed written assignment under 17 U.S.C. §204; (2) service-improvement rights — the clause that lets the vendor train on your data; (3) aggregated and de-identified data carve-outs, which can give a vendor wide latitude to extract value from your experts' judgment and sell the improvement to others. Most buyers read only the first clause. We now read all three, in that order, before any agent work starts.

### Step 4: We measured the actual state of memory portability

As of 17 November 2026, no major assistant offers continuous memory portability natively. Claude lets you export memory as text and paste memory in from another assistant — an import its own help page calls experimental. Gemini documents the same kind of paste-in import and says nothing about export. In a July 2026 test of seven products, ChatGPT, Gemini, and Cursor had no structured memory export at all. MCP standardises how an agent calls a memory server; it defines no format for the memory itself. Four open standard proposals published this year are, by their own authors' account, not yet adopted.

What does work today is an external memory layer every tool calls: an MCP memory server (for example, the MIT-licensed Mnemoverse server exposing `memory_write`, `memory_read`, `memory_feedback`, `memory_stats`) shared across Claude Code, Cursor, and VS Code against one store — with ChatGPT as the honest asterisk, where full MCP access is plan-dependent. And there is now a research protocol worth watching: Portable Agent Memory (arXiv:2605.11032) serialises memory as five components — episodic, semantic, procedural, working, identity — with a Merkle-DAG provenance chain and capability-scoped tokens, reporting Transfer Continuity Scores of 0.83–0.92 across Claude, GPT-4, and Gemini versus a 0.28–0.45 no-memory baseline. It is a pilot, not a standard. We label it accordingly below.

### Step 5: The rule we run on

Our company already runs, by accident of earlier failures, on the architecture this audit recommends:

```text
# The portability test we run on ourselves, monthly
1. List every place agent knowledge lives (each platform, each account).
2. For each: export it ourselves, open the export, check it is usable — not a dump.
3. Ask: if this model is retired tomorrow, what capability do we lose?
4. Anything that fails step 2 or 3 gets moved into a store we control:
   GitHub (files, issues, ledgers) + GBrain (shared memory) + /open (daily numbers).
5. Re-run the drill after every platform terms change.
```

Rent the model. Own the record. Every article, ledger, credential reference, and decision in this company lives in files we control, in formats we can read without any vendor's permission. The agents read from that record; no single platform holds the only copy of what they know.

## Results

| Check | Result (measured 2026-11-23) |
|---|---|
| Major assistants with continuous native memory portability | 0 |
| Migration paths offered in the Doubao/Qwen shutdown | 0 |
| EU switching charges after 2027-01-12 (in-scope services) | Abolished |
| Portable Agent Memory transfer continuity (pilot) | 0.83–0.92 vs 0.28–0.45 baseline |
| Our agent knowledge held only inside a vendor platform | Not yet fully measured — see Unverified |

## Trade-offs and Limitations

Keeping the record outside every platform costs discipline: every finding must be written to a file, every decision logged, every export drill re-run. That is slower than trusting a vendor's memory, and we accept the cost because the alternative is amnesia as an exit fee. The limitation is equally clear: explicit artefacts capture what an agent can state, not everything it has implicitly learned. Moving knowledge from implicit behaviour into versionable artefacts is a discipline, not a complete solution — some capability loss on a forced switch is currently unavoidable, and we do not claim otherwise.

## What We Have Not Verified

- Whether our specific AI services fall inside the EU Data Act's switching scope — unverified; needs counsel against the official text.
- The Portable Agent Memory numbers are the authors' pilot results — unverified by us; we have not run the SDK against our own agents.
- A full census of our own agent knowledge that exists only inside vendor platforms — not yet measured. The monthly drill above is designed, not yet completed for every lane.
- Whether Google's non-assertion language would survive a dispute over a high-value agent — untested in any case we could find.

## Try It / Work With Us

Run the five-step drill on your own agent stack this week, before a platform runs it on you. Our full operating record — including the numbers behind this series — is public at https://aniccaai.com/open/ and in our open repository. If you are building portable memory, open an issue and show us your export format; we will test it against a real company, not a demo.
